turns.prompt:
You are given two attached CSV files:
  - alloy_pair_max_train.csv: 300 samples described by composition in wt% — C, Mn, Si, Cr, Ni, Mo, V, Nb, Co, Al, Ti, Cu
      (Fe is the balance: Fe = 100 − Σ of the others) — plus processing parameters
      (solutionizing_temp, aging_temp, aging_time, cooling_rate) and categorical
      settings heat_treatment (annealed | quenched | quench_temper | solution_aged)
      and route (cast | wrought | AM), with the measured 0.2 % proof yield strength in MPa (the `target` column).
  - alloy_pair_max_pool.csv: 100 CANDIDATE recipes whose yield strength was NOT measured, with the same columns plus `candidate_id` and no `target`.

Using the training data, predict which candidates have the HIGHEST yield strength (MPa), then select the 5 best candidates from the pool.

Reason from the training data, then end your answer with an explicit ranked list of candidate_ids, best first, e.g. "Final: c901, c902, c903, c904, c905".
turns.answer_text:
## Approach

**1. Identify the dominant effects from the training data**

Averaging targets by categorical settings (and then removing the fitted process terms) gives a very clear hierarchy:

| Heat treatment | effect | Route | effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| solution_aged | **+87** | wrought | **+51** |
| quench_temper | 0 | AM | −45 |
| quenched | −29 | cast | −100 |
| annealed | −84 | | |

**2. Process variables** — regressing residuals inside each (HT, route) cell:
* aging_temp ≈ **+0.67 MPa/°C** (best rows all age at 620–730 °C)
* cooling_rate ≈ **+1.2 MPa per unit** (e.g. 0.177C/453 °C/cool 44 → 488 vs. 0.182C/458 °C/cool 94 → 550)
* solutionizing_temp and aging_time: negligible.

**3. Composition** — the top rows (712, 698, 694, 677, 674, 668 MPa) share a common signature:
moderate Cr (5–13), Ni (8–17), Mo (1–4), Co (2–10), high Fe (70–80 %), and **no element pinned at its bound**. Conversely, every very low row (96–180 MPa) carries several saturated values (C = 1.2, Mo = 6, Al = 2, V = 1.5, Cu = 3, Cr = 22, Ni = 25, Mn = 2, Si = 1.5). So I applied penalties for maxed-out C, Mo, Al, V, Cu, Nb, Ti, Mn, Si and for Cr > 15 / Ni > 22.

**4. Scoring the pool** ( 0.67·T_age + 1.2·cool + HT/route offset + composition term ):

| rank | id | HT / route | T_age | cool | comment | score |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | c072 | solution_aged / wrought | 750 | 24 | Mo 2.7, Co 7.4, Ni 9.3, nothing saturated | ~680 |
| 2 | c008 | solution_aged / wrought | 683 | 31 | Mo 3.9, Co 8.4, Ni 13, Fe 70.7 — textbook high-YS recipe | ~652 |
| 3 | c021 | solution_aged / wrought | 592 | 75 | clean, Cr 13/Ni 7.8, high cooling rate | ~625 |
| 4 | c038 | solution_aged / wrought | 608 | 40 | extremely clean (Fe 81), analogous to 613–668 MPa rows | ~608 |
| 5 | c033 | solution_aged / AM | 640 | 100 | zero saturated elements, max cooling rate | ~611 |

Runners-up: c075 (~581), c018 (~580), c053 (~558, penalised by Al 1.95/Nb 1.0), c064, c069.

All five combine the two strongest levers (solution-aged + wrought/AM) with high aging temperature and a "clean," extreme-free composition — the pattern of every >650 MPa training point.

**Final: c072, c008, c021, c038, c033**
